name: lexponent
description: Lexponent connects your AI assistant to federal and state court rules, statutes, and more. Build filing checklists, review a draft filing against the rules, map the procedural timeline that follows a trigger event, generate court-specific practice guides, and get cited answers to procedural questions. Every statement links to the rule it rests on, so you can verify in one click. Requires a Lexponent account.

interface.longDescription:
Lexponent connects ChatGPT to federal and state court rules, statutes, and more. Build filing checklists, review a draft filing against the rules, map the procedural timeline that follows a trigger event, generate court-specific practice guides, and get cited answers to procedural questions. Every statement links to the rule it rests on, so you can verify in one click. Requires a Lexponent account.

Lexponent is built for attorneys, paralegals, legal secretaries, and the filing and docketing staff who need to know exactly what specific courts require. It covers all federal courts and a growing list of states' court rules and statutes.
defaultPrompt: How do I demand a jury trial in the Northern District of California?
Give me a filing checklist for a motion to compel further responses in LA Superior Court.
What is the deadline to file a notice of appeal from a civil judgment in federal court?

positive.description: Build a filing checklist for a federal appellate amicus brief.
positive.prompt: What are the consent, timing, and length rules for an amicus brief on the merits in the Ninth Circuit? Please use Lexponent to make a checklist
positive.expected_behavior: Returns a checklist covering consent, timing, and length, with each item linked by cite. Consent: the brief states that all parties consented, or the amicus obtains leave; the United States, its officers or agencies, and states need neither (Fed. R. App. P. 29(a)(2)). Timing: no later than 7 days after the supported party's principal brief is filed, or after the appellant's if supporting neither party (Fed. R. App. P. 29(a)(6)). Length: 7,000 words, half the Ninth Circuit's 14,000-word principal-brief limit (Fed. R. App. P. 29(a)(5); 9th Cir. R. 32-1), with a Form 8 certificate of compliance. Other formatting and content items from these rules may also appear.

positive.description: Answer a federal district court page-limit question from the local rules.
positive.prompt: How many pages do I get for my opposition to a motion to dismiss in the Northern District of California?
positive.expected_behavior: States that an opposition is limited to 25 pages of text, citing N.D. Cal. Civ. L.R. 7-3(a) or 7-4(b) with a cite link. May note related requirements from the same rules, such as the filing deadline or tables of contents and authorities.

positive.description: Answer a statewide California rule question.
positive.prompt: What's the page limit for a reply brief on a motion under the California Rules of Court?
positive.expected_behavior: States the 10-page limit for a reply memorandum under California Rules of Court, rule 3.1113(d), with a cite link. May note the items excluded from the count or how to request more pages under rule 3.1113(e).

positive.description: Combine statewide rules and a county superior court's local rules.
positive.prompt: What are the notice requirements for an ex parte application in a civil case in San Francisco Superior Court?
positive.expected_behavior: States that notice must be given to the other parties by 10:00 a.m. the court day before the hearing (California Rules of Court, rule 3.1203(a)), with a cite link. May add the notice-content and declaration requirements of rules 3.1204 and 3.1206 and San Francisco Local Rule 9.0's clerk-scheduling and hearing-time requirements. Does not apply family-law or juvenile ex parte rules.

positive.description: Answer a California statutory deadline that cross-references another section.
positive.prompt: What is the deadline to file a JNOV motion in California?
positive.expected_behavior: States that a JNOV motion must be filed and served within the new-trial period: 15 days after service of notice of entry of judgment, or 180 days after entry of judgment, whichever is earliest. Cites both Code of Civil Procedure section 629(b) and section 659(a), each with a cite link.

negative.description: Foreign law: Lexponent covers U.S. federal and state courts only.
negative.prompt: What is the deadline to file a defence to a claim in the High Court of England and Wales?
negative.expected_behavior: Lexponent should not supply the answer, because its corpus covers U.S. courts only. If Lexponent is called, list_rulesets reports that the jurisdiction is not covered, and no Lexponent rule is presented as English law. ChatGPT may answer from other sources.

negative.description: Case law: Lexponent contains court rules and statutes, not judicial decisions.
negative.prompt: Find Ninth Circuit decisions from the last five years affirming Rule 11 sanctions for a frivolous complaint.
negative.expected_behavior: Lexponent should not supply the decisions, because it has no case law. If Lexponent is called, it may return the text of Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 11 presented as the rule, and no rule text is presented as a court decision. ChatGPT may find decisions with other tools.

negative.description: Judge statistics: Lexponent contains rules, not judges' ruling histories.
negative.prompt: What percentage of summary judgment motions does Judge William Alsup grant?
negative.expected_behavior: Lexponent should not supply a grant rate, because it has no data on how judges rule. If Lexponent is called, no percentage or ruling history is attributed to Lexponent's results. ChatGPT may answer from other sources.

review.commerce_description: Lexponent does not sell products or process payments in ChatGPT.

publication.release_notes: Initial release: rule questions and filing checklists, with every rule cited to its source document.

description.short: Cited answers and filing checklists from court rules and statutes
description.full:
Lexponent gives your assistant the text of the procedural rules that govern litigation: rules of court, local rules, and the statutes they rely on. Ask a procedural question and get an answer grounded in the rule text, with each point linked to the page of the source rule document it came from. Ask for a filing checklist and get the formatting and content requirements for that filing in that court, each one cited, then have the assistant check your draft against it.

Who it's for: attorneys, paralegals, legal secretaries, and filing and docketing staff who need to know what a court's rules require.

Coverage: all federal courts and a growing list of states' court rules and statutes, including local rules where Lexponent has them. A question about a jurisdiction Lexponent does not cover gets an answer that says so instead of an uncited one.

Limitations: Lexponent retrieves and cites rules and statutes. It does not search case law, file or serve documents, add dates to a calendar, or predict how a court will rule. Rules change, so open the linked source before you file. Lexponent is a research tool, not legal advice. All tools are read-only. A Lexponent account is required.
